title: F.W.J. Schelling and autopoiesis.
abstract: This paper explores certain conceptual resonances between Friedrich W. J. Schelling's philosophy of nature and a biological theory of autopoiesis developed by Humberto Maturana and Francisco Varela, and its subsequent extensions. While these frameworks emerged from different historical and intellectual traditions, they both challenge a mechanistic and reductionist understanding of life by emphasising self-organisation, the maintenance of boundaries, and relational autonomy. Schelling's dynamic monism describes nature as a self-productive process within which living beings arise through internal purposiveness, self-regulation, and resistance to external forces. Along similar lines, autopoiesis defines living systems as autonomous and self-producing networks which maintain their identity through structural coupling with the environment. Drawing on key notions such as cyclicity, reciprocal causality, embodied cognition, and self-representation, we argue that Schelling's philosophical approach towards the living can be viewed as analogical to many insights coming from the autopoietic theory.
journal: History and philosophy of the life sciences

title: A Tale of Two Principles-Towards a Relational Perspective on the Free Energy Principle.
abstract: The Free Energy Principle (FEP) offers a physically grounded account of intentional properties in mind and life, framed in the context of Dynamical Systems Theory. Because of this generality, it was proposed as a formal basis to formalize the study of biological autonomy, autopoiesis, and enactive cognition. Yet, those approaches are centered by definition on describing how biological and cognitive agents are "laying down a path in walking", or (re)constructing their own biological/cognitive structure through engagement with the world. Drawing from Rosen's relational biology, we argue that such processes are by construction outside a "Newtonian" description in terms of well-defined observables and their dynamics. Rather, we draw from the thermodynamics of observation and biological computation to demonstrate the emergence of contextuality: the participatory production of observables against which the agent regulates their activity. We suggest a complementarity between Friston's classical FEP and Fields' relational FEP, describing, respectively, the dynamics within a biological/cognitive space and the construction of that space. Finally, we propose a structural realist understanding of this complementarity where both principles act on a physically embedded system of biological constraints, rather than an abstract mathematical space assumed to fully represent biological/cognitive organization.

title: The computational genesis of a self: Representational time and self-modeling in living systems.
abstract: The transition from inanimate physicochemical dynamics to autonomous agency represents a fundamental challenge across theoretical biology and cognitive science. While traditional accounts have approached this transition through descriptive frameworks of autopoiesis, anticipatory systems, or the free energy principle, a formal deductive derivation linking computational irreducibility to functional agency has remained elusive. Here, a deductive framework demonstrates that core attributes of biological agency, specifically representational time, forward predictive processing, and self-modeling, emerge as operational necessities for an autonomous agent persisting within a computationally irreducible environment under a defined operational regime of delayed hazards and counterfactual pre-commitment. Grounded in organizational closure and viability theory, this framework establishes three principal deductive results. First, it is demonstrated that purely reactive behavioral strategies fail under observationally aliased environmental states requiring mutually incompatible viability-preserving actions; persisting under delayed viability hazards without lethal trial-and-error mandates the internal synthesis of a tripartite representational time. Second, this representational time is shown to share the operational organization of counterfactual forward prediction. Third, drawing upon closed-loop regulator theory, the Conant-Ashby theorem, and the internal model principle, it is established that evaluating candidate interventions over extended horizons (H > 1) in a coupled system requires internalizing the agent's own generative action dynamics, yielding a functional self-model distinct from simple state-dependent regulation. These formal derivations are subsequently grounded in concrete molecular and cellular phenomena, including cyanobacterial KaiABC timekeeping, synthetic protocellular clocks, microbial adaptive regulation, and bacterial chemotaxis, explicitly demarcating experimentally demonstrated substrates from theoretical extrapolations. Finally, the framework develops a theoretical bridge connecting computational irreducibility to the semiotic hypothesis of organic codes as physical adaptors bridging decoupled biological domains, incorporating the code-mediator-artifact distinction. The analysis concludes that within the specified operational regime, functional self-representation emerges as an inevitable computational consequence of autonomous persistence.

title: Genealogies of organizational closure: from logical paradox to mind in life.
abstract: Organizational closure occupies a central position in contemporary theories of autonomy, anticipation, agency, sense making, and the continuity between life and mind. Its investigation has given rise to a diverse landscape of related explanations, including closure to information, cyclic closure, operational closure, semantic closure, closure-to-efficient causation, metabolic closure, and closure of constraints. Although each of these explanatory approaches captures important aspects of organizational closure, their proliferation has often generated conceptual ambiguity. As a result, organizational closure is frequently conflated with feedback loops, recursive algorithms, self-organization, or biochemical cycles. This paper develops a genealogical conceptual analysis of the research programs from which these various accounts emerged, tracing their origins across mathematical logic, first- and second-order cybernetics, general systems theory, thermodynamics, metabolic theory, relational biology, and the biology of cognition. In doing so, it provides a principled framework for assessing the commitments involved whenever a notion of closure is invoked, while clarifying the origins of these explanations and the relations among them. Particular attention is devoted to the roles of self-reference, circular causality, replication maps, semantics, free energy, automata, operations, and constraints in shaping the current understanding of organizational closure. On this basis, the study advances the interpretative thesis that organizational closure is most coherently understood as a circular organization of efficient causes through which living beings continuously produce and maintain the conditions of their own existence. From this perspective, organizational closure appears irreducible to purely algorithmic descriptions inherited from the Church-Turing thesis-not because living beings cannot be simulated in specific respects, but because the causal production of the conditions of their own realization cannot be exhaustively characterized as a state-determined syntactic procedure. This interpretation helps clarify the distinctions between organizational closure and the notions with which it is often conflated, while providing a framework for assessing current debates concerning artificial intelligence, large language models (LLMs), semantic meaning, and sense making in the face of ambiguity and logical paradox.

title: Experimental probes of autopoietic self-maintenance.
abstract: Autopoietic closure is a constitutive causal property of a living system: a recursively organized network produces the components and boundary conditions that regenerate that same network. Experiments can reveal, discriminate, or fail to detect this organization, but they do not create or define it. This article develops a categorical account of the relation between autopoietic organization and its experimental representation. Building on a topos-theoretic formulation of viability-localized self-production, the paper distinguishes three levels: the natural biological system, a formal organizational surrogate, and the observer-side profile generated by experimental protocols. A category of organizational models and a category of typed protocols are defined explicitly, together with a realization functor from protocols to formal test objects. The Yoneda lemma then characterizes formal models through all formal tests, while restriction to an experimentally available protocol family yields a partial response profile. Equivalence of restricted profiles establishes organizational equivalence only when that protocol family is conservative on a specified class of candidate models. This condition converts the idea of an adequate assay panel into a precise, model-relative criterion without conflating experimental accessibility with operational closure. The framework also distinguishes diagnostic from predictive uses, accommodates destructive assays, differentiation, environmental context, and one-off experimental histories, and limits its claim about emergence to local-to-global compatibility. A worked reaction-network example shows how perturbation profiles discriminate highly resilient from fragile self-maintaining organizations while the causal closure remains defined by the reaction network itself. The result is an experiment-oriented semantics for testing formal models of autopoietic self-maintenance, not an observational redefinition of autopoiesis.

title: Aging as cross-hallmark obstruction amplification: A sheaf-theoretic model of repair closure, senescence, inflammation, and regenerative failure.
abstract: The twelve hallmarks of aging describe heterogeneous molecular, cellular, tissue, and systemic changes but do not by themselves explain how they become an organism-level loss of repair capacity. Aging is represented as a cost-constrained, stochastic loss of autopoietic repair closure. Hallmark processes are organized as coupled local-to-global constraint layers on a finite biological complex: global sections represent compatible repair modes, while a connecting morphism measures when coherent regulatory states generate material-repair incompatibilities. The principal accounting identity states that coupled repair reserve equals material-repair closure plus regulatory-interface closure minus cross-hallmark obstruction rank. The identity follows from standard exact-sequence and rank-nullity arguments; its biological content lies in the construction of the coupled aging object and the interpretation of obstruction rank as cross-hallmark repair incompatibility. A dynamical extension places repair under finite, fallible control, stochastic perturbation, delayed feedforward dependence, and an explicit viability domain, allowing additional surveillance to reduce global repair when coupling costs exceed local gains. A reproducible two-compartment example specifies stalk variables, restriction maps, coboundary matrices, H<sup>0</sup>, H<sup>1</sup>, connecting-map rank, and an approximate persistence interval. Published epigenetic-clock, skeletal-muscle regeneration, and senolytic results are literature-anchored mappings rather than empirical validation. The proposed invariants therefore target one structural dimension of aging: loss of achievable, globally compatible repair under finite biological control.

title: Formalizing autopoiesis: Toward a Categorical-Thermodynamic Calculus of Closure.
abstract: The concept of autopoiesis, introduced by Varela and Maturana (1974) to characterize the organizational closure shared by all living systems, has remained an open challenge for rigorous mathematical treatment. This paper traces Varela's formalization program from Spencer-Brown's calculus of distinctions through the Arithmetic of Closure and Form Dynamics, to the emergence of the Eigenform as a fixed-point model of biological identity. We analyze the methodological gap between this deterministic algebraic framework and the stochastic dynamics characteristic of living systems, and identify it as the central open problem motivating contemporary post-Varelian research. As a programmatic proposal rather than a completed formal system, we outline a Categorical-Thermodynamic Calculus of Closure that would integrate lambda-calculus fixed-point operators, topological category theory, and variational free energy minimization into a common setting for autopoietic systems under thermodynamic noise. We position this proposal within the contemporary cartography of autopoiesis, restrict its scope to autopoiesis in its strict organizational sense, and maintain a clear distinction between autopoietic organization and its formal representation. Rather than claiming a finished formalization, we identify the primitives, open problems, and evaluation criteria that such a formalization would require, and discuss the direction this sets for theoretical biology, cognitive science, and the foundations of autonomous systems.

title: Organizational closure through regenerative signaling as a possible basis for conscious awareness.
abstract: Along the lines of neuronal global workspace theories, the paper hypothesizes that active neural signal regeneration in recurrent, re-entrant circuits could constitute an organizational basis for states of conscious awareness. In this view, brains are self-production systems that regenerate their own informational, signal states ("neural autopoiesis"). States of awareness themselves depend critically on sustained regeneration of sets of neural signals in local and global circuits. The set of regenerated signals at each moment determines the specific contents of consciousness. Two hypotheses are proposed. H1: Organizational closure and with it, awareness, is achieved when regenerative, self-production loops are completed, such that a stable set of signal productions is sustained. The organization of informational processes stabilizes and closes on itself. H2: Neural coding is critical for signal regeneration. Neural signals must be properly encoded in order for them to be regenerated and thereby affect the contents of awareness. In addition to simple signal suppressions at their points of origin, one means by which general anesthetic agents may abolish awareness is by scrambling neural signals. Rendering internal control signals incoherent by altering within- and across-neuron rate profiles and/or temporal patternings may disrupt signal regeneration in local and global circuits. The two hypotheses are agnostic with respect to neural coding. Our own signal-centric time-domain (TD) brain theory framework is presented to illustrate how signal regeneration could be mediated by local and global temporal codes and neural temporal processing networks. Similarities and differences between TD, global neuronal workspaces (GNW), recurrent processing (RP), integrated information (IIT) and predictive processing (PP) are discussed. Empirical testing will necessitate solving the neural coding problem at multiple system levels. This will involve investigating correlations and causal linkages between regeneration of tracked neural signals and states of awareness as well as between alternative candidate neural codes and the contents of awareness. Rhythm-tagged stimuli and high temporal resolution neural recordings are proposed to enable tracking of specific neural signals throughout the brain under conditions of waking vs. sleep vs. anesthesia, with masking and unmasking signal/noise levels. Some philosophical comments regarding organization as a potential basis for consciousness are made.

title: Autopoiesis: The organizational closure of social systems
abstract: <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title><jats:p>The attempt to define living systems in terms of goal, purpose, function, etc. runs into serious conceptual difficulties. The theoretical biologists Humberto Maturana and Francisco Varela realized that any such attempt cannot capture what is distinctive about them: Their autonomy and unity. Goal, purpose, etc. always define the system in terms of something extrinsic, whereas living systems are unique because they maintain their unitary continuity of pattern despite the ceaseless turnover of their components. So, system‐closure is a prerequisite of their adequate conceptual comprehension. Maturana and Varela themselves found that system‐closure pertains exclusively to their organization, i.e. the set of relations among system‐components which unify them. For living systems this comprises the relation between the system‐components and the processes which they undergo. This relation is self‐referential because it is closed, i.e. it essentially (re)produces itself.</jats:p><jats:p>While this model worked very well in the biological domain, attempts to extend it to the social domain met with serious conceptual obstacles. The reason for this is that Maturana did not make a consistent enough application of it. He understood the components of social systems biologically (individuals, persons, etc.) and the relations between them socially (language). This inconsistency ruptured the system's organizational closure. Consequently organizational closure (autopoiesis) can be maintained only when both the components of social systems and their processes are of the same type: Social. This interpretation can be found in the work of Niklas Luhmann who recognizes that the components of social systems are not persons, individuals, actors or subjects but communicative actions themselves. This preserves the organizational closure of the system and permits the concept of autopoiesis to be used as a powerful instrument of social analysis.</jats:p>

title: What Simulation Discloses: Emergence, Organizational Closure, and Autopoiesis in Self-Modifying Systems
abstract:
<jats:p>This paper examines what simulation discloses about emergence, organizational closure, and autopoiesis in selfmodifying systems. Computational experiments in artificial life can do philosophical work by making explicit and testable the organizational assumptions built into these concepts. We use the Compositional Disclosure Model (CDM), a self-modifying computational system with a second-order cybernetic structure, in which the organization acts on its own operative repertoire, as a bounded conceptual case study. The system discovers macro-actions through compositional graph reasoning and verifies organizational closure through modal temporal logic. The experimentâ€™s philosophical contribution lies in the question it makes tractable: when an agent discovers a forward-right diagonal action by composing forward and right movement primitives, has it discovered something genuinely new, or merely disclosed what was always latent in the relational structure of its base schema? We argue that emergence in simulation is characteristically a matter of disclosure rather than creation, a shift from latent relational structure to manifest organizational form. We further argue that disclosure is a semiotic event: a latent relation becomes operative under an interpretive criterion and, once admitted, revises the horizon of subsequent action. Formal verification functions here not as proof of life but as epistemic scaffolding, making organizational assumptions explicit, comparable, and revisable. Across repeated runs, the disclosed action structure yields stable organizational consequences. The central claim is therefore methodological as much as metaphysical: computational experiments of this kind can transform disputes about emergence and organization into disciplined, revisable objects of inquiry.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Data/Code available at: https://github.com/Ohara124c41/computational-disclosure-models</jats:p>
journal: ALIFE 2026: Proceedings of the 2026 Artificial Life Conference

title: Operationalizing autopoiesis beyond organisms via repair-closure
abstract: <jats:p>We propose a perturbation-testable criterion for organizational autonomy beyond organisms: \emph{repair-closure}, the ability of a system to restore the constraints that constitute its organization after targeted perturbations within a bounded horizon.We develop a proof-complete framework in which viability is a local-to-global consistency problem and viable regimes are global sections of a viability subsheaf (a structure enforcing local-to-global consistency) over a finite compartment complex.To ground the theory biologically, we provide a worked ecosystem-module example inspired by the sulfidic chemoautotrophic Movile Cave system, specifying candidate constraints, concrete perturbation protocols, measurable readouts, and plausible repair pathways.We distinguish geological boundaries from internally maintained \emph{functional boundaries} and prove that repair-closure implies invariant maintenance of such boundaries under perturbation.We formalize openness via explicit interfaces and prove persistence of coupled viability under slack witnesses.Finally, we give an implementable computational pipeline and quantitative Lipschitz--slack radii that turn robustness claims into explicit parameter neighborhoods.</jats:p>

title: Closure Without Enclosure: Fungal Mycelia and the Distributed Form of Autopoiesis
abstract: <jats:p>Autopoietic organization persists by producing and repairing the components and boundary conditions that realize the network of production itself. Filamentous fungi provide a stringent distributed case: a mycelium grows through moving apical production fronts, continuously remodels its wall, externalizes part of digestion into the surrounding substrate, reallocates resources through a changing network, regulates cytoplasmic continuity through septa, fuses only under recognition constraints, and may maintain multinuclear or heterokaryotic organization. The formalization retains viability localization, monadic production/repair, boundary production, admissibility, and viable global regimes as the defining autopoietic semantics. Fungal transport, wall, regulatory, nuclear, and fusion layers are coupled by limits and internal relations; when layerwise production/repair realizations are available, their coupling is formed in the Eilenberg–Moore category so that the composite inherits a canonical realization without assuming linear state spaces. Local-to-global viability is governed by sheaf descent. Environmental substrate transformation is represented in a slice topos, separating produced fungal interfaces from extracellular transformation while preserving relative autopoietic closure. Growth, fusion, injury, and repair are represented by correspondences between changing mycelial bases and internal viability relations; viable identity is existence of a section of the resulting history object, not persistence of fixed anatomy. Septal plugging changes descent conditions, anastomosis requires recognition-admissible effective descent, and mycorrhizal exchange is a pullback coupling between distinct closures. This architecture yields discriminating empirical tests: organization-aware interface measurements should predict survival, fusion, and symbiotic persistence beyond morphology alone; matched morphologies may have different viable outcomes; and reducing connectivity can restore viable continuation after local damage. Filamentous fungi therefore instantiate closure without enclosure and expose biological individuality as continuity of viability-localized self-production across changing boundaries.</jats:p>

title: Business Autopoiesis Through Process Referencing
abstract: <jats:p>In this chapter, the concept of autopoietic system is assumed to stem from the theory of social communication systems, which reproduce all their specific structures and self-referential processes. This chapter aims at the analysis of business process development and management. The main goal is to present an original framework of business process management. Through this framework, business processes can be interpreted as autonomic artifacts which are created, discovered, explored, and disseminated within social communities of practice. This constant reproduction of processes and their dissemination allows the social organization to exist, cope with internal complexity, and achieve its operational goals. The chapter consists of three main parts. The first part covers the systematic literature review on business process mining and referencing. The second part includes the discussion on presented business process framework. The last part comprises a case study to present and discuss the application of the framework for the development of academic virtual education processes.</jats:p>
journal: Advances in Human Resources Management and Organizational Development

title: Viruses as Living Systems? Borrowed Closure and the Limits of Autopoiesis
abstract: <jats:p>In 2022, Yolles and Frieden argued that viruses are alive by moving the criterion for life from metabolism to organisation, arguing the genome–capsid couple to be autopoietic. This study reframes that conclusion with two constructs of Fisher-Generative Informational Realism (FGIR): the CAS/CAAS boundary, separating a Complex Adaptive System (CAS), adaptive but not self-sustaining, from a self-sustaining Complex Adaptive Autopoietic System (CAAS); and the coercivity law, which requires a system’s protoenergy, the informational effort of holding a configuration in persistent form, to exceed a threshold. The verdict “viruses are not autopoietic” conflates two conditions. Viruses satisfy the topological condition, the couple being a genuine self-producing network, but fail the resourcing condition, since the capacity to maintain it belongs to the host: “borrowed closure”, which we derive formally. Identifying the viral protoenergy with the draw on the host, and letting self-supply return only when the lineage’s translation machinery is complete, yields a host-budget equation with a saddle-node bifurcation at a critical completion fraction. Given a near-all-or-nothing return of self-supply, the barrier is structural rather than statistical, and it survives stochastic, epidemiological and delayed reformulations; its value is illustrative. The account is falsifiable and taxonomically agnostic, as the ribosome-encoding but host-dependent bacterium Carsonella ruddii shows, and crossings into self-sufficiency are observed only downward.</jats:p>

title: Viability-Localized Autopoiesis II: An Operator Calculus for Probes, Contexts, Scale Translation, and Empirical Closure Tests
abstract: <jats:p>A preceding BioSystems article formulated autopoiesis as viability-localized self-production: biological closure is evaluated after viability localization, production and repair are represented by a generative realization structure, boundary maintenance is made explicit, admissible boundary states constrain production, and at least one viable global regime must exist. The present article develops the second stage of that framework. It does not redefine autopoiesis. It develops an operator layer for analyzing how a specified autopoietic datum is probed, compared across contexts, transported across scales, extended from partial data, and tested against empirical constraints.The paper introduces an autopoietic operator system composed of a viability-localized autopoietic core together with probe families, context fibrations, descent data, scale-translation operators, data-extension operators, and diagnostic signatures. The main result is an operator-insufficiency theorem: fixed points, monads, sheaves, admissibility predicates, internal languages, context fibrations, adjunctions, Kan extensions, and Yoneda profiles are individually insufficient to analyze viability-localized autopoiesis, because each misses at least one relevant failure mode. These include production failure, boundary-admissibility failure, local-to-global gluing failure, context dependence, scale-translation distortion, and probe-relative indistinguishability.The operator calculus is anchored in standard biological data structures and workflows: flux balance analysis in the BiGG E. coli core model, epithelial cyst and lumen assays, viral host-factor dependence, planarian perturbation-response profiles, ecological feasibility networks, metabolic model reduction and reconstruction, and single-cell reference mapping. A reproducible flux-balance calculation shows that aerobic glucose, anaerobic glucose, and pyruvate-dehydrogenase-blocked conditions all admit viable global flux sections in the E. coli core model, but with distinct biomass objectives and context defects. The result is an operational continuation of viability-localized autopoiesis: the first stage specifies what counts as autopoietic closure, and the present paper specifies how such closure is interrogated by probes, contexts, scale changes, and empirical data.</jats:p>

title: Formalizing autopoiesis: Toward a Categorical-Thermodynamic Calculus of Closure
The Coercivity Law of Enaction Within Fisher-Generative Informational Realism: A Cybernetic Threshold for Autopoietic Closure
abstract: When does a complex adaptive system (CAS) (like a thermostat, a market, a flock, or a large language model) become a complex adaptive autopoietic system (CAAS), one that actively produces and sustains itself rather than merely adapting to its environment? We argue that this transition requires two simultaneous conditions. The first, established in a companion work, is architectural sufficiency. The system’s decision structure must achieve recursive closure at the third cybernetic order, the so-called fractal-seed point. The second, derived here, is corporeal viability. The system must pay a structural cost (the enactment tension E) large enough to hold its organization in place against perturbation. Working within Fisher-Generative Informational Realism (FGIR), an informational-realist framework in which information, not matter or energy, is the primary generative substrate of reality, we derive a scalar invariant E = Ipc2, where Ip is the integrated informational potential of the operative field and c is the global coherence conductance at which informational structure locks into place. This invariant marks the threshold at which a proto-autopoietic system crosses into full autopoiesis. Because FGIR treats physical mass-energy as the result of a freezing projection acting on an incorporeal informational manifold rather than as the foundation of reality, the same invariant that governs autopoietic closure in social and organizational systems also projects, under appropriate bridge conditions, for instance, onto the classical physical law E^=m^ c^2, or in a quantum context, the Schrödinger equation. The physical projection is stated as a conditional equivalence (T-BRIDGE), but it is not the focus of this paper. Rather, the central contribution is the cybernetic threshold itself and its operationalization. We show how a systems theorist can assess a system’s distance from critical admissibility, even when the absolute magnitudes of Ip and c are unavailable in domains that lack R(6) closure; we connect the coercivity threshold explicitly to Ashby’s Law of Requisite Variety, supplying the energetic constraint that Ashby’s purely combinatorial criterion leaves implicit. The contemporary case of large language models illustrates the framework. LLMs display transient, externally-scaffolded R(3)-like decision structure but fail the coercivity threshold, and so remain proto-autopoietic. The paper thus offers systems science a derived criterion, additional to architectural closure, for distinguishing full from proto-autopoiesis, with a specified but as yet unexecuted test program across physical, biological, cognitive, and social domains.

title: Intelligence without Experience: Autopoietic Agency and the Organizational Conditions of Consciousness
abstract: Recent advances in artificial intelligence have reignited the debate over whether artificial systems may eventually develop consciousness. This paper challenges the assumption that intelligence, agency, and consciousness constitute successive stages along a single developmental continuum, arguing instead that they are conceptually distinct phenomena. Drawing on Maturana and Varela’s concept of autopoiesis, it is argued that adaptive self-maintaining organization is sufficient to explain capacities such as learning, adaptation, and goal-directed behavior without presupposing subjective experience. The paper further proposes that consciousness requires additional organizational conditions beyond those underlying intelligence and agency. By distinguishing subjective experience from adaptive functionality, this framework provides a more rigorous basis for assessing claims about machine consciousness and their ethical and governance implications.

The Wave and the Torus: Why Integrated Information Is Grain Diversity, Not Scalar Consciousness
Requisite Variety, Autopoiesis, and Self-organization
abstract: Ashby's law of requisite variety states that a controller must have at least as much variety (complexity) as the controlled. Maturana and Varela proposed autopoiesis (self-production) to define living systems. Living systems also require to fulfill the law of requisite variety. A measure of autopoiesis has been proposed as the ratio between the complexity of a system and the complexity of its environment. Self-organization can be used as a concept to guide the design of systems towards higher values of autopoiesis, with the potential of making technology more "living", i.e. adaptive and robust.

title: Continuous closure, axes closure, and natural closure
abstract:
Let $R$ be a reduced affine $\mathbb C$-algebra, with corresponding affine algebraic set $X$. Let $\mathcal C(X)$ be the ring of continuous (Euclidean topology) $\mathbb C$-valued functions on $X$. Brenner defined the \emph{continuous closure} $I^{m cont}$ of an ideal $I$ as $I\mathcal C(X) \cap R$. He also introduced an algebraic notion of \emph{axes closure} $I^{m ax}$ that always contains $I^{m cont}$, and asked whether they coincide. We extend the notion of axes closure to general Noetherian rings, defining $f \in I^{m ax}$ if its image is in $IS$ for every homomorphism $R 	o S$, where $S$ is a one-dimensional complete seminormal local ring. We also introduce the \emph{natural closure} $I^
atural$ of $I$. One of many characterizations is $I^
atural = I + \{f \in R: \exists n >0 	ext{ with } f^n \in I^{n+1}\}$. We show that $I^
atural \subseteq I^{m ax}$, and that when continuous closure is defined, $I^
atural \subseteq I^{m cont }\subseteq I^{m ax}$. Under mild hypotheses on the ring, we show that $I^
atural= I^{m ax}$ when $I$ is primary to a maximal ideal, and that if $I$ has no embedded primes, then $I = I^
atural$ if and only if $I = I^{m ax}$, so that $I^{m cont}$ agrees as well. We deduce that in the polynomial ring $\mathbb C[x_1, \ldots, x_n]$, if $f = 0$ at all points where all of the ${\partial f \over \partial x_i}$ are 0, then $f \in ( {\partial f \over \partial x_1}, \, \ldots, \, {\partial f \over \partial x_n})R$. We characterize $I^{m cont}$ for monomial ideals in polynomial rings over $\mathbb C$, but we show that the inequalities $I^
atural \subset I^{m cont}$ and $I^{m cont} \subset I^{m ax}$ can be strict for monomial ideals even in dimension 3. Thus, $I^{m cont}$ and $I^{m ax}$ need not agree, although we prove they are equal in $\mathbb C[x_1, x_2]$.

title: Beyond SIFT using Binary features for Loop Closure Detection
abstract: In this paper a binary feature based Loop Closure Detection (LCD) method is proposed, which for the first time achieves higher precision-recall (PR) performance compared with state-of-the-art SIFT feature based approaches. The proposed system originates from our previous work Multi-Index hashing for Loop closure Detection (MILD), which employs Multi-Index Hashing (MIH)~\cite{greene1994multi} for Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) search of binary features. As the accuracy of MILD is limited by repeating textures and inaccurate image similarity measurement, burstiness handling is introduced to solve this problem and achieves considerable accuracy improvement. Additionally, a comprehensive theoretical analysis on MIH used in MILD is conducted to further explore the potentials of hashing methods for ANN search of binary features from probabilistic perspective. This analysis provides more freedom on best parameter choosing in MIH for different application scenarios. Experiments on popular public datasets show that the proposed approach achieved the highest accuracy compared with state-of-the-art while running at 30Hz for databases containing thousands of images.

title: Internal Neighbourhood Structures II: Closure and closed morphisms
abstract: Internal preneighbourhood spaces inside any finitely complete category with finite coproducts and proper factorisation structure were first introduced in my earlier paper. This paper proposes a closure operation on internal preneighbourhood spaces and investigates closed morphisms and its close allies. Consequently it introduces analogues of several well known classes of topological spaces for preneighbourhood spaces. Some preliminary properties of these spaces are established in this paper. The results of this paper exhibit preneighbourhood systems are more general than closure operators and conveniently allows identifying properties of classes of morphisms independent of continuity of morphisms with respect to induced closure operators.

title: Matrix orbit closures
abstract: Let $G$ be the group $GL_r(C) \times (C^\times)^n$. We conjecture that the finely-graded Hilbert series of a $G$ orbit closure in the space of $r$-by-$n$ matrices is wholly determined by the associated matroid. In support of this, we prove that the coefficients of this Hilbert series corresponding to certain hook-shaped Schur functions in the $GL_r(C)$ variables are determined by the matroid, and that the orbit closure has a set-theoretic system of ideal generators whose combinatorics are also so determined. We also discuss relations between these Hilbert series for related matrices, including their stabilizing behaviour as $r$ increases.

title: Simulated Autopoiesis in Liquid Automata
abstract: We present a novel form of Liquid Automata, using this to simulate autopoiesis, whereby living machines self-organise in the physical realm. This simulation is based on an earlier Cellular Automaton described by Francisco Varela. The basis of Liquid Automata is a particle simulation with additional rules about how particles are transformed on collision with other particles. Unlike cellular automata, there is no fixed grid or time-step, only particles moving about and colliding with each other in a continuous space/time.

title: Equilibrium Selection and Closure in DSGE Solution Methods
abstract: Standard DSGE solution practice closes forward-looking equilibrium problems by combining model specification with criteria that select one operational equilibrium from multiple candidate paths, yet this closure step typically remains implicit. This paper formalizes that closure step as a substantive operation in standard DSGE solution practice. By separating the economic specification ($S$), the self-referential operator ($T$), and the equilibrium selection rule ($Π$), the $(S, T, Π)$ triad provides a descriptive semantic grammar for comparing closure choices across familiar solution environments. The framework clarifies what standard solver diagnostics actually report, captures the regime-iteration logic of piecewise-linear methods like OccBin, explains why independent linear solvers often reproduce the same selected equilibrium, and distinguishes within-model refinements from specification-augmenting closure changes under indeterminacy.

title: Information Measures of Complexity, Emergence, Self-organization, Homeostasis, and Autopoiesis
abstract: This chapter reviews measures of emergence, self-organization, complexity, homeostasis, and autopoiesis based on information theory. These measures are derived from proposed axioms and tested in two case studies: random Boolean networks and an Arctic lake ecosystem.   Emergence is defined as the information a system or process produces. Self-organization is defined as the opposite of emergence, while complexity is defined as the balance between emergence and self-organization. Homeostasis reflects the stability of a system. Autopoiesis is defined as the ratio between the complexity of a system and the complexity of its environment. The proposed measures can be applied at different scales, which can be studied with multi-scale profiles.
